description: Reviews, testimonials and rating displays: the social proof a homeowner reads before picking up the phone. Shows the aggregate score from a platform they trust, then a few short, believable reviews from neighbours.
queries: single large testimonial quote section with customer photo
local business reviews section with star rating
interior design studio client testimonials section

references.layout: Full-width saturated band. Tiny monospace eyebrow top-left, serif headline under it (~40px), then three equal portrait cards (~3:4, ~16px radius). Each card is a full-bleed exterior photo of a home; a frosted-glass panel inset ~12px from the card edges fills most of the card and holds a large quote, with name + town/state at bottom-left and a tiny icon at bottom-right.
references.type: Transitional serif for headline and quotes, regular weight, tight leading (~1.1); quotes set near display size (~26px). Eyebrow in monospace caps ~10px, wide tracking. Attribution small sans ~10px.
references.color: Background ~#1E3A8A deep cobalt; headline ~#B9CCF5 pale blue instead of white; frosted panels ~rgba(255,255,255,0.15) with backdrop blur; quote text ~#FFFFFF.
details: Eyebrow reads 'WHAT HOMEOWNERS SAY', naming the audience instead of saying 'Testimonials'
Headline is two short sentences with full stops: 'Real homes. Real savings.'
Attribution is first name + initial + town, state (e.g. 'Norwood, MA'), so the location does the proving
Each photo shows a real house at golden hour, so the image persuades before the words do
Quotes are short (12-20 words) and set huge; there are no stars at all
references.why_it_works: A house photo with a short serif quote reads like a magazine feature, not a review widget. Naming the town makes it believable.
references.trade_adaptation: Roofers, solar, painters, window installers: one finished-exterior photo per card, quote pulled from a Google review, attribution 'Dana R. · Westlake'. Three cards on desktop, horizontal swipe on mobile.

references.layout: Two rows on a warm off-white page with faint vertical grid lines in the side margins. Top row: left half has a pill eyebrow, a serif headline, a short paragraph and a dashed-outline button; right half holds a Trustpilot score card drawn as a stack of three slightly offset paper cards. Then a centred 'Excellent rating' label sitting in a gap of a hairline divider, then three unboxed review columns (serif name + inline star boxes, then ~4 lines of body).
references.type: Serif headline ~28px regular with the key phrase in italic ('past clients'); reviewer names serif ~16px; body sans ~12px at ~1.6 leading; pill eyebrow sans ~10px.
references.color: Background ~#FBF8F4; text ~#1F2A33; italic accent teal ~#1F7A7A; eyebrow pill fill ~#DCEFEF; stars in platform green ~#00B67A; dashed button border ~#7FBFBF on ~#DFF1F1.
details: The score card is a little stack of paper (two offset outlines behind it), which makes a third-party badge feel physical
Two words of the headline in italic serif with an accent colour
'Excellent rating' sits inside a break in the hairline, like a label on a printed form
Reviews have no cards and no avatars: just name, stars and text
The dashed button border repeats the stacked-paper outline
references.why_it_works: It leads with the aggregate score from a platform people recognise and follows with three short real reviews, which is how people judge a local service. The quiet palette keeps it credible.
references.trade_adaptation: Swap Trustpilot for a Google card ('4.9 ★ · 312 Google reviews'), headline 'Hear from our neighbours', three recent reviews signed first name + last initial. Ideal for plumbers, HVAC, pest control.

references.layout: Laid out like an editorial table. A small 'From our customers' label sits top-left; the condensed headline, a two-line intro and two buttons start at column 2 (~1/3 in). Below that, full-width rows divided by hairlines: the left ~1/3 holds the client name (bold ~12px) and role/company (grey ~10px), the right holds the quote (~18px) and a small 'Read more about what we've done →' link.
references.type: Headline in a heavy condensed grotesk, all caps, ~36px, tight; quotes in condensed sans ~18px regular at ~1.35 leading; labels ~11px.
references.color: White ~#FFFFFF ground, near-black ~#141414 text, hairlines ~#D9D9D9; primary button filled stone ~#C9C2B0 with black text, secondary button outlined black.
details: Every quote links to the project it came from ('Read more about what we've done')
The buttons under the headline are 'See completed projects' and 'Book a meeting', so the section also converts
Attribution has its own column, so all quotes share one left edge
No photos and no stars; the length and specificity of the quotes carry the credibility
references.why_it_works: It treats testimonials like a firm's client list: serious, easy to scan and tied directly to finished projects, which is how contractors actually win work.
references.trade_adaptation: Remodelers, landscapers, roofers: name + neighbourhood + job type in the left column ('Kitchen remodel · Oak Park'), quote on the right, link to the matching gallery project. Strong fit for an industrial or premium style.

references.layout: Centred serif headline above four equal portrait cards (~3:4, ~10px radius) in one row. Each card is a video still of a customer looking at the camera in their own home, with a translucent play button (~44px circle) in the middle and a bold name line plus a one-line story caption at bottom-left over a dark gradient.
references.type: Headline transitional serif ~36px regular, second sentence in italic and accent colour; captions sans ~11px with the name in bold.
references.color: Cream ground ~#FCF6EC; headline ~#2A2522; italic accent rust ~#B4573A; play button ~rgba(255,255,255,0.35); caption gradient to ~rgba(0,0,0,0.5).
details: Headline pattern 'Real people. Real results.' with the second half in italic and colour
Captions describe an outcome ('From diabetes diagnosis to action') instead of a star rating
Subjects are filmed in their own homes in natural light, not as studio headshots
The play button is translucent so the face stays the focus
references.why_it_works: Video of real people in real rooms is the strongest form of proof, and the cream, rust and serif treatment keeps it warm rather than corporate.
references.trade_adaptation: Short phone-shot clips of homeowners in the finished kitchen or next to the new furnace; caption 'Maria · Flooded basement to finished den'. Use stills with the same caption if there is no video.

references.layout: Heavy slab-serif 'Reviews' title top-left (~44px). Under it, the left third shows 4.9 + stars + review count and a 5-row histogram, the middle shows '97% would recommend these products', and the right third is a 5×3 mosaic of square customer photos. After a rule, reviews run as rows: reviewer column (initials avatar, name, location, verified, item) | 1px black divider | stars, bold title, body, helpful votes | a ~100px customer photo on the far right.
references.type: Display slab/soft serif ~44px in black weight; review titles ~13px medium; body sans ~11px.
references.color: Cream ~#FBF9EF ground; black ~#111111 text, histogram bars and 1px rules; customer photos supply the only colour.
details: A mosaic of customer photos sits right next to the score, putting visual proof beside the number
'97% would recommend' is written as a plain sentence with a bold number
A thick black vertical divider separates reviewer details from the review
Reviewers without photos get black circles with white initials, so the list stays consistent
references.why_it_works: It combines the aggregate score, the distribution and customer photos in one band, and the strong black-on-cream type makes a dense block feel designed.
references.trade_adaptation: For a full reviews page: Google score + histogram, a mosaic of job photos customers sent in, then reviews tagged by service ('Water heater install'). Suits bold and friendly styles.

references.layout: Stacked rows that alternate sides. Each row puts a candid vertical photo (~260×390, ~10px radius) on one side and the quote block, vertically centred, on the other: a pull-quote (~24px medium, 3-4 lines), a short story paragraph (~11px), then the name in bold and 'Member since 2018'.
references.type: Rounded grotesk throughout; pull-quote ~24px medium at ~1.15 leading; body ~11px regular; name ~12px semibold.
references.color: Cream ~#FFFBEA ground; text dark teal ~#1E4747; peach header band ~#F4AE85 above the section.
details: The photos are customers' own holiday snaps: casual, imperfect and believable
The pull-quote is the outcome in plain words ('Paid off in one trip.'), and the paragraph gives the context
A tenure line ('Member since 2018') replaces a job title
About 120px of space between rows, so each story stands on its own
references.why_it_works: One customer, one photo, one outcome. It reads like a profile rather than a widget, and the candid photo makes it feel human.
references.trade_adaptation: 'Customer since 2009' for HVAC maintenance plans or pest control; photo of the family on their porch or in the new bathroom; the pull-quote is the outcome ('No more ice dams.').

references.layout: A single rounded panel (~16px radius) across the content width, ~190px tall, with everything centred: a small quote glyph, a one-line quote set as a headline (~34px), then a tiny avatar + name + role inline.
references.type: Condensed grotesk in heavy/black weight ~34px with tight tracking; attribution ~11px.
references.color: Peach panel ~#FDD0AE on a warm grey page ~#F0EEE9; quote mark rust ~#C2410C; text ~#1A1A1A.
details: The whole testimonial is seven words, edited down to a headline
The quote mark is small and coloured rather than a giant decorative glyph
The avatar is a tiny (~28px) rounded square beside the name, not a big circle
references.why_it_works: It makes the boldest choice available: pick one line and set it like a headline. It also works as a pause between denser sections.
references.trade_adaptation: 'They showed up when they said they would.' in a heavy condensed face on a tinted band. Fits between the services section and the quote form on any trade page.

references.layout: One black-framed card (~370×380) centred on a pale grey page. The upper ~60% is a studio portrait inset inside a ~8px black border; the lower ~40% is solid black and holds the quote (~20px), a small grey attribution and a tiny spark glyph at bottom-right. The subject's hands and chair continue below the card edge.
references.type: Neo-grotesk regular ~20px in white; attribution ~9px grey ~#8A8A8A.
references.color: Page ~#E6E8EA; frame and text area ~#000000; quote ~#FFFFFF.
details: Portrait and quote share one continuous black frame, so it reads like a printed poster
The subject's body extends past the frame for depth
Plain typographic curly quotes, no oversized quote glyph
references.why_it_works: It gives one hero testimonial a gallery-like presentation, and the frame is easy to reproduce in CSS.
references.trade_adaptation: For a high-end remodeler or custom landscaper: portrait of the homeowner in the finished space inside a charcoal frame, quote below. Use once per page.

references.layout: A full-width hairline on top. Left half: 'Reviews' (~32px bold) with a one-line intro. Right half: stacked rows divided by hairlines, each with the platform name (bold ~20px, underlined), a row of large black stars (~18px) with the numeric score, and 'N reviews as of DATE' in small text.
references.type: Geometric grotesk; title ~32px bold; platform names ~20px bold; meta ~11px regular.
references.color: White ground; black ~#000000 stars and type; hairlines ~#D0D0D0.
details: Each rating carries a date ('354 reviews as of 6/1/2022'), which reads as honest
Stars are monochrome black, not yellow
Platform names are underlined links to the source
Half stars are drawn precisely (4.4 shows four and a bit)
references.why_it_works: It is the simplest credible way to show several review platforms, and the monochrome stars look editorial rather than salesy.
references.trade_adaptation: Rows for Google, Yelp, Angi and BBB, each with score, review count and an 'as of' date, linking out. Good for minimal and industrial styles.

references.layout: Three centred columns with no cards: a tiny 5-star row on top, the quote (~13px) centred over 3-5 lines, then the first name in bold and a grey qualifier ('Age 54') underneath.
references.type: Sans ~13px regular for quotes; names ~10px bold; qualifier ~10px regular.
references.color: Cream ~#FBF6EC ground; text ~#2A2522; stars rust ~#B4573A at ~8px each.
details: Stars are tiny and tinted in the brand rust, not yellow: present but quiet
A two-word qualifier under the name gives context
No avatars and no boxes; whitespace does the separating
references.why_it_works: Calm, honest and fast to read. It shows how holding back makes reviews feel less manufactured.
references.trade_adaptation: First name + neighbourhood or job ('Tom · Furnace replacement') with tiny stars in the brand accent. Drops into the homepage of any style.

references.layout: Centred section title; three equal cards (~190×150, ~4px radius, soft shadow), each a different muted tint. The quote is the card headline (~18px bold, coloured), followed by the name in bold + 'worked with: …' and a row of small grey tag chips naming the services involved.
references.type: Grotesk; quote ~18px bold with tight leading; attribution ~10px; chips ~8px.
references.color: Section ~#FCF1EC; card tints peach ~#F6CDBE, sage ~#D6DDCF, blue-grey ~#C6D7DC; each quote in a darker shade of its own tint: orange ~#E2683A, green ~#6E8F67, teal ~#1F6F8B.
details: Quote text is a darker tone of its own card tint (tonal), never black
Service tag chips under each review say what was done
Quotes are under 15 words so they can be set large
references.why_it_works: The tonal tinted cards look designed and friendly, and the service tags turn praise into information about what the business does.
references.trade_adaptation: Tags like 'Panel upgrade' and 'EV charger' for electricians, or 'Spring cleanup' and 'Patio' for landscapers; take the card tints from the trade's palette.

references.layout: A full-width masonry wall of about four columns of review cards (avatar, name, role, quote) that fades out at the top and bottom. One solid card is pinned dead-centre over the wall: a big '4.9', five stars, 'Based on 50+ G2 reviews' and the platform logo.
references.type: Score ~36px light; card text sans ~12px; meta ~9px monospace.
references.color: Near-black ~#121212 ground; cards ~#1C1C1C with ~#2A2A2A border; text ~#CFCFCF fading to ~#555555 at the edges; centre card ~#0F0F0F with crisp white type.
details: The wall is deliberately dimmed so it reads as volume rather than something to read
One crisp aggregate badge floats above it and is the only thing in focus
Card heights follow quote length, so the masonry looks natural
references.why_it_works: It shows quantity and quality at once: the faded wall says 'lots of people', the badge says 'and they rate us 4.9'.
references.trade_adaptation: Light-mode version for trades: a faded wall of real Google review snippets behind a centred '4.9 ★ · 486 Google reviews' card with a 'Read them all' link.

takeaways: Lead with the aggregate (score + count + platform), then show about three short real reviews. Never put more than ~6 on a homepage.
Attribute locally: first name + last initial + town or neighbourhood, plus the job done, beats job titles and avatars.
Edit quotes hard. The best sections set a 7-20 word quote at display size instead of paragraphs in small type.
Real photos of the customer or their finished home do more than stars. With no real photo, use no photo rather than a stock avatar.
Keep stars quiet: small, monochrome or tinted with the brand accent, not saturated yellow.
Tie praise to work: link the quote to the project or tag the service performed.
Cite and date the rating source ('as of', 'on Google') so the numbers read as honest.
One typographic accent (an italic serif phrase or a coloured second sentence) is enough to make the heading feel crafted.
avoid: Grid of identical white cards, each with a circular stock avatar, five yellow stars and 'John D., CEO' (Fresha, Kalstore, Blue Apron)
Giant decorative quotation-mark glyphs floating behind the text
Carousels with arrows and dots that hide all but one review
Walls of embedded tweets with @handles and bird icons, which read as SaaS
E-commerce review widgets with sort, filter and 'was this helpful?' votes on a marketing homepage (Glossier, KÖPPEN, Hims)
Stock headlines like 'What our customers say' or 'Don't just take our word for it'
Corporate job titles in attribution where a neighbourhood or job type would mean more to a homeowner
